Subject Robert Sandeman Lamb (British).

Made by D.S.I. Logan. Forwarded by D.L. Crawford.

Reference letter dated July 17th 1940 from
H.B.M. Consulate-General, Passport & Registration
Office, asking for information concerning R.S. Lamb,
enquiries have revealed the following:-
Robert Sandeman Lamb (British) is reported
to have served as a junior officer in the Indian
Army or Air Force during the Great War. After the
end of the Great War he is reported to have been
in Canada and the U.S.A., where he worked for
General Motors. From U.S.A., he is stated to have
gone to Japan where he also worked for General Motors.
Sometime prior to 1934, he came to Shanghai where he
subsisted precariously for some time. In 1936 he
was employed as business manager of the Cathay
Cosmopolitan, a monthly publication, the aims of
which were claimed to be the "provision of an
"independent forum for the expression of opinions
"on all manner of subjects pertaining to the economic,
"political and commercial life of this great
"community."

Associated with Lamb in this publication
were George M. Dallas (American) Editor; Ian Black
Douglas, Associate Editor. Other contributors to
the publication were Mario Rocchi; Angus J.N. Herba
and Paul Paelz. Paul Paelz subsequently became a

partner of Lamb in the publication. According to
information obtained at time of the first appearance
of this monthly magazine (January 1936) it was
subsidized by the South Manchurian Railway, Maj.
General Tsogai of the Kwantung Army and Paul Paelz
who was alleged to have had access to the funds of
the German and Italian Legations. Note: Paul Paelz
is now known to be an active agent of the Nazi Party
in Shanghai.

Lamb was in 1935-6-7, a frequent contributor
of letters to "The People's Tribune" under the
pseudonym "Junius Simicus." Perusal of these letters
reveals them to be mostly of the type that seeks
to expose rackets and social evils.

The Cathay Cosmopolitan ceased publication
after the outbreak of Sino-Japanese hostilities in
1937. On August 6th 1937, a quarrel over a cheque
took place between Lamb and Paelz, in the office of
the Cathay Cosmopolitan, Room 521, 128 Museum Road,
which resulted in Lamb assaulting and injuring Paelz
to the extent that he had to be treated in the General
Hospital. Paelz, however, chose not to charge Lamb
as they had to wind up the business of the magazine.
At this time they shared a room in the New Asia Hotel.
On March 31st 1937, Lamb also came to the notice of
the Police in connection with a letter which he wrote

1935、1936及1937年间，兰姆经常以笔名“Junius Simicus”向《人民论坛报》（The People's Tribune）投稿信件。查阅这些信件显示，其内容大多旨在揭露敲诈勒索团伙和社会弊病。

1937年中日敌对行动爆发后，《华夏环球》停刊。1937年8月6日，兰姆与佩尔茨在博物馆路128号521室的《华夏环球》办公室内因一张支票发生争执，导致兰姆殴打并致伤佩尔茨，伤势严重至需在总医院接受治疗。然而，佩尔茨选择不对兰姆提出指控，因为他们当时正需结束杂志的业务。此时，他们合住在新亚酒店（New Asia Hotel）的一个房间内。1937年3月31日，兰姆也因写给

Lamb also came to the notice of the Police

兰姆在上海英国法院被控以虚假手段获取价值197.00元的食品饮料一案，于1934年12月6日被驳回。

1935年8月30日，兰姆也因一起车费纠纷殴打并致伤一名公共人力车夫而引起警方注意。然而，兰姆向该车夫支付了赔偿金，车夫遂撤回了指控。

在当地，兰姆被认为是一个好斗、大嗓门的人，几乎对任何话题都能夸夸其谈。他将各位领事官员以及当地知名的商界和专业人士称为自己的亲密朋友，并给人留下印象，仿佛这些人中的某一位正在幕后操纵为他谋取一份确凿的好工作，

Lamb has a habit of getting into debt but
usually succeeds, by means of his glib speech, in
getting one of his acquaintances to settle his
accounts. Despite his permanent lack of ready money,
he regularly contrives to get drunk but much of the
liquor he consumes he obtains by forcing his company
on casual acquaintances. As far as can be ascertained,
he has had no regular employment since 1937 but is
stated to have done casual jobs of accounting and
editing around the city.

Lamb was formerly a member of the Shanghai
Engineers Club, Room 500, 220 Szechuen Road but was
recently expelled, due to failure to pay his debts.
Through his membership of this Club, he made the
acquaintance of Mr. F.A. Naylor, Secretary & Treasurer
of the Club. Late one night about the end of
September or beginning of October, 1939, he appeared
outside Naylor's flat, Room 704, 220 Szechuen Road

LETTERS OF JUNIUS SINICUS
A NOTE TO THE READER

Normally Junius Sinicus attempts to preserve in his communications a standard of language and style not inconsistent with the name he has adopted. Even in his most abusive moments he has kept his abuse dignified, and has not descended to a mere vulgar and ignorant calling of names. If, in the following letter, he departs from that rule, and adopts the language of the gutter, it is because he wishes his remarks to be understood by the individual to whom they are addressed, and any other language would, it is feared, be far above his head.

* * *

TO CARROLL D. ALCOTT, ESQ.,
Radio Commentator and Blackmailer.
c/o "The China Press"
Shanghai.

HOWDY AL!—This, I believe, is how your fellow Americans usually address you, so lest you fail to recognize any more polite form of address I am adopting the same contemptuous familiarity.

You will no doubt wonder what prompted this letter. The fact is that the other day I came across in the dictionary, the word—PEST, meaning "Troublesome or destructive person, animal, or thing." and somehow I immediately thought of you. Before my mind's eye appeared the face (or should I, to make sure you really understand, say "mug") of a slackly obese individual, who by some strange freak of Providence has been permitted to plague the community which he has infested. This may not speak very well for the community in question, but seeing that this very community contains a large proportion of parasitic, anaemic individuals who thrive on the offal which pests exude, it need not be a matter for great surprise, though it is certainly one for considerable regret.

In hygienic and well-ordered communities, pests are not in the least welcome and I for one am whole-heartedly for their extermination here. You know, Al, you may be a little tin-god (or brass-horn) to some of your listeners-in, but not to all of them. Decent people like good clean things, not pests, and they cannot forget all the things of which you are a foul composition, which definitely place you in the latter category.

通常，朱尼厄斯·西尼库斯试图在其通讯中保持与其所采用的名字相称的语言和文体标准。即使在他最谩骂的时刻，他也保持着谩骂的体面，没有降格为 mere 粗俗无知的辱骂。如果在下面的信中，他背离了这一准则，采用了下流社会的语言，那是因为他希望收信人能理解他的言论，而恐怕其他任何语言都远远超出了此人的理解能力。

致卡罗尔·D·奥尔科特先生，
电台评论员兼敲诈者。
转交《大美晚报》
上海。

你好啊，阿尔！——我想，这是你的美国同胞通常称呼你的方式，所以，以免你无法识别更礼貌的称呼形式，我采用了同样轻蔑的亲昵口吻。

你无疑会想知道是什么促使我写这封信。事实是，前几天我在字典里查到了“PEST”（害虫/讨厌鬼）这个词，意思是“令人烦恼或具有破坏性的人、动物或事物”，不知怎么的我立刻想到了你。在我眼前浮现出一个松弛肥胖者的脸孔（或者为了让你真正明白，我是否该说“丑脸”），由于某种奇怪的命运捉弄，此人被允许折磨他所侵染的社区。这可能对有关社区来说不是什么光彩的事，但鉴于这个社区包含大量靠害虫排泄的污物为生的寄生、贫血个体，这也就不足为奇了，尽管这确实令人相当遗憾。

在卫生良好、秩序井然的社区中，害虫完全不受欢迎，而我本人全心全意支持在此将其消灭。你知道，阿尔，对你的部分听众来说，你可能是一个小神像（或铜管乐手），但并非对所有听众都是如此。正派人士喜欢干净美好的事物，而不是害虫，他们无法忘记构成你那肮脏本质的所有东西，这些东西明确地将你归入后一类。

JUNIUS SINICUS

When you first came here from some low dive in gangster-ridden Chicago, you were much slimmer, it is true, but you already had all the ear-marks of a pest, and a fairly poisonous one at that. It did not take you very long to settle down to a racket. A gullible editor, American, of course, gave you a “lift”, and you were assigned to cover the courts. That was a Heaven-sent gift, as nothing could have suited your racket better. At that time, some fifteen years ago, there were still a few modest souls in this city who shrank from the glare of publicity, especially if this publicity arose from a divorce suit. These meek souls presented fine, red meat for you, the Ravenous Pest. Your sharp ears listened avidly to all the evidence produced in court, and all that was not told in court you obtained from unscrupulous lawyers (especially from a certain bearded specimen of the species). All the sordid details (including a great deal of imaginative matter divulged by embittered husbands, wives or third parties to the inevitable triangle) were carefully collected, after which you prepared for the kill. Silence and suppression of publicity were often very welcome to divorcing parties, and you did not have much difficulty in making them pay for suppression of the news in your bag. In fact, you usually got all the necessary dope beforehand from the lawyers, and got your “fees” even before the court hearing. It was certainly a lovely racket, and an illustrious example of American journalism as practised by an illustrious member of the American Fourth Estate.

Unfortunately for you, your racket did not last very long. You got up against an irate husband once, a strong man who did not in the least care whether you published news of his divorce or not, and moreover, strongly objected to your blackmailing methods. Besides giving you a good hammering, he also reported your actions to the police. It was a matter of touch-and-go for you, and prison-bars loomed uncomfortably close, but some smart lying on your part, coupled with “moral” support from the bearded lawyer referred to above, saved you from being a public liability. Some pests really bear charmed lives!

Your narrow escape put the brakes on your unholy ambitions, and you tried to settle down to straight journalism. But it was tough going, Al, wasn’t it? No nice, fat pickings, and therefore no good whoopee times. Yes, it sure was tough! Banging away at a typewriter all day long (for a paltry 150 dollars a month), and parading the streets for news, was not at all to the liking of a Pest.

Opportunity, however, came knocking round your door again pretty soon after that. Of course, Al, you remember your old pal

朱尼厄斯·西尼库斯

当你最初从帮派横行的芝加哥某个低级窝点来到这里时，你确实瘦得多，但你已经具备了害虫的所有特征，而且是一种相当有毒的害虫。你没花多长时间就安顿下来搞起了敲诈勾当。一位容易上当的编辑——当然是美国人——给了你一次“提拔”，你被指派负责报道法庭新闻。那真是天赐良机，因为没有什么比这更适合你的敲诈行当了。那时，大约十五年前，这座城市里还有一些谦逊的灵魂回避公众关注的目光，特别是如果这种关注源于离婚诉讼的话。这些温顺的灵魂为你这只贪婪的害虫提供了鲜美的红肉。你敏锐的耳朵 avidly 聆听着法庭上提出的所有证据，而法庭上未提及的内容，你则从无耻的律师那里获取（尤其是从该物种中某个留胡子的典型代表那里）。所有肮脏的细节（包括由愤恨的丈夫、妻子或不可避免的三角关系中的第三方披露的大量虚构内容）都被仔细收集起来，随后你便准备下手“宰杀”。沉默和压制 publicity 往往非常受离婚双方的欢迎，你毫不费力地让他们为你袋中的新闻保密付费。事实上，你通常事先就从律师那里得到了所有必要的内幕消息，甚至在开庭审理前就拿到了你的“酬金”。这确实是一个美妙的勾当，也是美国第四等级的一位杰出成员所实践的美国新闻业的辉煌典范。

不幸的是，你的勾当并没有持续很久。有一次你惹怒了一位丈夫，那是一个强壮的男人，他根本不在乎你是否公布他的离婚新闻，而且强烈反对你的敲诈手段。他不仅把你痛打了一顿，还向警方报告了你的行为。对你来说，情况千钧一发，监狱的铁窗 uncomfortably 地逼近，但你凭借一些聪明的谎言，加上上述那位留胡子律师的“道德”支持，使你免于成为公共负担。有些害虫确实有着受庇护的生命！

你的死里逃生给你的不法野心踩了刹车，你试图安下心来从事正当的新闻工作。但这很艰难，阿尔，不是吗？没有肥美的猎物，因此也没有快乐的时光。是的，确实很艰难！整天敲打字机（每月仅得微薄的150美元），并在街头奔波寻找新闻，这完全不符合一只害虫的喜好。

然而，机会很快又敲响了你的门。当然，阿尔，你还记得你的老伙计

Beaumont alias Israelovitch, (there always seems to be a little Jew about), and his high-powered manipulations in this city. Among Beaumont's numerous ventures, which included motor-cycle dirt track speeding and cycle racing, (which flopped when he failed to obtain the license for pari-mutuels and other gambling devices from which he planned to make money), was a yellow sheet called the "Shanghai Spectator." Your pal Beaumont had to beat it rather hastily one fine day, and left all his ventures in the gutter, so to speak, including his yellow sheet. It wasn't a very difficult job for you to pick up the said yellow sheet, because, as we understand it, pests usually crawl in gutters.

Thus, finally, your heart's desire was satisfied, and we find a real, live pest seated in an editorial chair in a rather lousy, but still an editorial sanctum.

The "Shanghai Spectator," before it fell into Beaumont's hands and later into your pestiferous grip, was a social and sporting publication, but Beaumont changed all that, and used the publication's "socialite" subscription list to direct some nasty diatribes against some of the city's social lights some of whom may have deserved all that comes to them. Beaumont, however, was doing it out of spite because they wouldn't give him a gambling license for his cycle racing. The "Spectator" was also little Beaumont's (he only stood five feet one in his stockinged-feet) campaign weapon—campaign for election to the select coterie of this city, the Shanghai Municipal Council. Beaumont, as I'm sure you remember, wanted to be elected a Councillor so that he could get himself granted all the gambling licenses he wanted. But the scheme didn't work! It was a flop!

As editor your chest swelled with pride now. You say you made a success of the publication, when you picked it up out of the gutter, of course. Well, yes and no. If you mean that you made more money out of it, perhaps; although no appreciable improvement was noticeable in your personal appearance—which was in full correspondence with your muck-raking habits. It's all a question of standards, that is, about the amount of money you made out the "Spectator." You might have made less than Beaumont did, but thought it was more, because your requirements are less. You remember, of course, that Beaumont lived like a prince—champagne, a luxurious apartment, a swell limousine and "peachy dames." But you—you were satisfied with Hongkew whiskey, dirty dumps and tough dames. Every man to his taste, naturally, so we don't blame or criticise you. Anyway, except a Pest cannot be expected to have very high-class tastes.

致卡罗尔·D·奥尔科特 3

博蒙特，别名伊斯雷洛维奇（似乎总有点犹太血统），以及他在这座城市的高能操纵手段。在博蒙特的众多 ventures 中，包括摩托车泥地竞速和自行车赛（当他未能获得计划从中获利的 pari-mutuels 和其他赌博设备的许可证时，这些项目就失败了），还有一份名为《上海观察家》的小报。有一天，你的伙计博蒙特不得不匆忙溜走，把他所有的 venture 都扔进了阴沟，可以说，包括他那份小报。对你来说，捡起这份所谓的小报并不是什么难事，因为据我们所知，害虫通常在阴沟里爬行。

于是，最终，你的心愿得到了满足，我们发现一只真正的、活生生的害虫坐在一间虽然相当破旧、但仍是编辑圣殿的编辑椅上。

《上海观察家》在落入博蒙特手中以及后来落入你那害虫般的魔掌之前，是一份社交和体育刊物，但博蒙特改变了这一切，并利用该刊物的“社交名流”订阅名单，对该市的一些社交名流发表了一些恶毒的攻击文章，其中一些人可能罪有应得。然而，博蒙特这样做是出于怨恨，因为他们不给他自行车赛的赌博许可证。《观察家报》也是小博蒙特（他穿着袜子身高只有五英尺一英寸）的竞选武器——竞选进入本市精选的小圈子，即上海公共租界工部局董事会。博蒙特，正如我确信你记得的那样，想当选为董事，以便为自己获取所有想要的赌博许可证。但这个计划没成功！是个失败！

作为编辑，你现在自豪地挺起了胸膛。你说当你从阴沟里捡起它时，你使这份出版物取得了成功，当然。嗯，既是也不是。如果你是指你从中赚了更多的钱，也许吧；尽管你的个人外表没有明显的改善——这与你的揭黑习惯完全相符。这全是一个标准问题，也就是说，关于你从《观察家报》中赚了多少钱的问题。你赚的可能比博蒙特少，但你认为更多，因为你的要求较低。你当然记得，博蒙特过着王子般的生活——香槟、豪华公寓、高级轿车和“漂亮女人”。而你——你满足于虹口的威士忌、肮脏的住所和强悍的女人。人各有好，自然如此，所以我们不责怪或批评你。无论如何，除了害虫不可能指望有很高的品味。

JUNIUS SINICUS

Talking about wine and women, we nearly forgot the progress you made with the "Spectator." We're hard put to find the exact word for the racket which you then practised, but for want of a better, we'll use an old-fashioned word, Blackmail. Ugly word, you say, but really there's none uglier we can think of at the moment. The game was tried out by you in diverse ways, and there were many victims, but the most succulent ones turned out to be certain ladies who operated certain establishments. According to the sanctimonious ruling of the Settlement's august ruling body, the Council, brothels—to be blunt—were taboo, and no licenses were issued for such establishments. However, this was no deterrent for certain enterprising ladies and they clandestinely operated such houses. The "Spectator," in righteous indignation decided to uproot this public evil. They would publish full data of all these illicit houses, and the publicity would force the Council to take appropriate action. Oh, yes, Al, you did give them some publicity. We remember that some photographs of these establishments were published in your crusading journal,—photographs of the entrances or parts of the buildings, without the house numbers showing. The dodge was to scare the ladies into a belief that their houses were going to be closed. This is when our Pest enters the picture, by a side door. Driven by pity, the Pest offers a nice little solution out of the impasse. "If you'll only be so kind as to pay me for my trouble, I'll see that no more adverse publicity gets into my magazine," says the Pest to the worried ladies. And, of course, they paid. A very, very easy way to pay for publication costs and earn a soft living. We wonder what St. Boniface would have said if he had investigated this angle of the lives of women with lost souls.

This racket lasted some time, Al, but our burg did not offer unlimited fleecing opportunities, and finally you had to fold up and back went the "Spectator" to the gutter whence it came. And back went Al, the Pest, to his old reporting job.

It was another tough break for you, Al, and we realize how much you missed the flesh-pots, but never say die—pests are pretty virile and manage to exist in the most odoriferous and obnoxious surroundings. And thus it was with you. The editorial rooms of the "China Press," which received you like a prodigal—without the trimmings, unfortunately, for you had to labour and sweat for a paltry one hundred and seventy-five dollars—seemed gloomy and unwholesome, even to a pest like yourself. But there was nothing else to be done. The Fourth Estate had got you in a pretty strong grip, although you had many lapses—long and unaccountable absences in tough Hong-

4
朱尼厄斯·西尼库斯

谈到酒和女人，我们差点忘了你在《观察家报》方面取得的进展。我们很难找到一个确切的词来形容你当时实践的勾当，但由于找不到更好的词，我们将使用一个老式的词：敲诈。你说这个词很难听，但目前我们想不出更难听的词了。你以多种方式尝试了这个游戏，受害者众多，但最肥美的受害者竟是某些经营特定场所的女士。根据租界最高统治机构工部局的庄严裁决，妓院——坦率地说——是被禁止的，此类场所不发执照。然而，这对某些进取心强的女士来说并不是阻碍，她们秘密经营此类房屋。《观察家报》怀着义愤，决定根除这一公害。他们将公布所有这些非法房屋的完整资料，而 publicity 将迫使工部局采取适当行动。哦，是的，阿尔，你确实给了它们一些 publicity。我们记得你的 crusading 期刊上刊登了这些场所的一些照片——入口或建筑物部分的照片，但没有显示门牌号。这种伎俩是为了吓唬这些女士，让她们相信她们的房子将被查封。这时，我们的害虫从侧门登场了。出于怜悯，害虫提供了一个摆脱困境的小妙招。“只要你们好心地付给我麻烦费，我就保证我的杂志上不再出现任何不利的 publicity，”害虫对焦虑的女士们说。当然，她们付了钱。这是一种非常、非常容易支付出版成本并赚取舒适生活的方式。我们想知道，如果圣博尼法斯调查过这些迷失灵魂女性的生活的这一方面，他会说些什么。

这个勾当持续了一段时间，阿尔，但我们这座城市提供的无限剥削机会有限，最终你不得不收摊，《观察家报》又回到了它来的阴沟。阿尔，这只害虫，也回到了他旧的报道工作岗位上。

对你来说，阿尔，这是又一次沉重的打击，我们意识到你是多么怀念那些享乐之地，但永远不要气馁——害虫生命力相当顽强，能够在最臭气熏天和令人厌恶的环境中生存。你就是这样。《大美晚报》的编辑室像迎接浪子一样接待了你——可惜没有附带待遇，因为你必须为微薄的175美元辛勤劳作和流汗——即使对你这样的害虫来说，这里也显得阴郁和不健康。但也别无他法。第四等级已经牢牢控制了您，尽管您有许多过失——在艰难的虹口长期且无法解释的缺席——

page_data.en:
TO CARROLL D. ALCOTT 5
kew dives. You know, Al, cheap whiskey and tough women are really bad for the system, even for the system of a Pest. However, that's neither here nor there.
When this city was shattered by a few nasty bombs in August 1937, it seemed to be the prelude for a regular incursion of pests into the foreign-controlled areas. There were small pests and big pests. Some managed to exist for a while, but most of them were "Flit-ted" out of existence. We then thought that even some of the old, hardened pests like yourself would not have much chance of existence, but you seemed to bear a charmed life, and one fine day while tuning in to catch the strains of some beautiful soul-inspiring music, what was our disappointment to hear over the ether the raucous croaking of a whiskey-hoarsened voice. Curiosity got the better of us and we finally realized that our old friend, the Pest, had taken on a new role.
We have no great admiration for people of this city, and when we learned that the Pest was listened to by quite a large audience we were not in the least surprised. It didn't take us long to cotton on to your new racket. Criminal racketeering, such as that practised in Chicago and other American cities, had long gone out of style, and had given place to political racketeering. You must be given some credit for taking up the cue so rapidly, but then Pests adapt themselves to changed conditions in no time.
If we had been told some years ago that you would one day fill the role of loud-speaker for certain political interests, we would have laughed outright, as we all know that you have neither the education nor the capabilities to fill such a role. You must have reformed and done some hard studying to be able to differentiate Washington from Napoleon, and New York from Timbuctoo. Apart from your rather expressive slang, your blarings over this city's ice creamy radio station are characterized by a daily demonstration of that ignorance and lack of education which is so well-known to most of the city's editors and copy-readers.
It certainly speaks volumes for the mentality of the men connected with certain political circles that they are willing to make use of the services of a bum and former crook (pardon my frankness, but I believe that you Americans like straight-from-the-shoulder talk) to air the political views of their respective governments. It's a question of taste, of course, or rather, poor taste.
In spite of all your present political veneer, however, you don't seem to have lost any of your old propensities. Our little city was all a-jitter recently over the notorious Riley case, and what would all our little ham-burgers have to say if they knew how you tried to

基夫·戴夫斯。你知道的，阿尔，廉价威士忌和泼辣女人确实对身体有害，哪怕是对像你这种“害虫”的身体也是如此。不过，那都是题外话。
当这座城市在1937年8月被几枚可恶的炸弹炸得支离破碎时，这似乎预示着各类“害虫”将常规性地入侵外国控制区。有小“害虫”，也有大“害虫”。有些设法苟活了一阵子，但大多数都被“飞力”（Flit）杀虫剂消灭了。当时我们以为，就连一些像你这般老资格、顽固的“害虫”也没有多少生存机会，但你似乎命硬得很。有一天，当我们调谐收音机，准备聆听一些美妙且鼓舞人心的音乐旋律时，却失望地通过电波听到一个因威士忌而嘶哑的粗嘎嗓音。好奇心战胜了我们要，我们最终意识到，我们的老朋友，“害虫”，已经扮演了一个新角色。
我们对这座城市里的人并无太多敬意，因此当我们得知听“害虫”广播的受众相当庞大时，一点也不感到惊讶。我们没花多久就弄清了你的新勾当。像芝加哥和其他美国城市那样实行的刑事勒索团伙活动早已过时，取而代之的是政治勒索。你如此迅速地抓住这一线索，倒该给你记上一功，不过话说回来，“害虫”总是能瞬间适应变化的环境。
如果几年前有人告诉我们，你总有一天会充当某些政治利益的扩音器，我们会放声大笑，因为众所周知，你既没有受过教育，也没有能力胜任此类角色。你一定是改过自新并刻苦攻读，才能分辨出华盛顿与拿破仑的区别，以及纽约与廷巴克图的不同。除了你那颇为生动的俚语外，你在本市这家“冰淇淋”广播电台上的叫嚣，其特点在于每日都在展示那种为本市大多数编辑和校对员所熟知的无知和缺乏教养。
这无疑充分说明了与某些政治圈子有关联的那些人的心态，他们竟然愿意利用一个流浪汉和前罪犯（请原谅我的直率，但我相信你们美国人喜欢直来直去的谈话）来宣扬各自政府的政治观点。这当然是一个品味问题，或者更确切地说，是品味低劣的问题。
然而，尽管你现在披上了政治外衣，你似乎并未丧失任何旧有的习性。最近，我们这座小城因臭名昭著的莱利案而人心惶惶，如果那些小市民们知道你是如何试图

ham-string Crook Riley, in the good old-fashioned way you formerly
used, and that when that failed you double-crossed the “s!ot-machine
king”?

Now don't squirm, Al, but bear with me a little longer. We just
happen to know that you approached Riley some time last June with
a proposition to suppress any adverse “publicity” which might crop
up in the local press, not failing to mention that through your own
underworld connections you were in possession of all the “dope”
worth knowing about Mr. Riley. But Riley was riding the top of the
wave, and he told you to go to hell and take your cheap blackmailing
tactics with you. That settled the matter for Riley. From that
time onwards, not a single week passed without mention of Riley
and his gambling ventures appearing in Benjie Powell's yellow rag,
the “China Weekly Review.” or the “China Press.” Both Benjie
and yourself failed to get any dough from Riley, so that two of you
went gunning for him in a big, bad way—otherwise, in typical Amer-
ican Wild West fashion.

Well, Riley's in for it, but neither you nor Benjie are richer
for the experience. Yes, Al, just another tough break, and just
imagine what you would have done with all that dough which you
thought was coming to you. Better luck next time!

Of course, radio “commentatoring” is not too bad with the extra
income it provides you, not taking into account the two hefty body-
guards which you have to employ at your own expense, but somebody's
going to win the war pretty soon, and that somebody is definitely
not among the boys backing your radio braying. Perhaps you'd
better take our tip and quit this radio business and save your lungs
for some other purpose—shouting out ads for “Flit” and other
similar insecticides, for instance. You know, “Flit,” etc., are darned
good for eliminating pests. Personally, we like “Flit” and we won't
forget to use it against pests, especially one—with a raucous voice
and sloppy figure.

Adios!

JUNIUS SINICUS.

用你以前惯用的老派手段去废掉骗子莱利的双腿，并且在失败后又背叛了那位“老虎机大王”，他们会作何感想呢？

好了，别坐立不安，阿尔，再忍耐我一会儿。我们碰巧知道，去年六月某时，你向莱利提出了一项提议，要求压制当地报纸上可能出现的任何不利“宣传”，并特意提到，通过你自己的黑道关系，你掌握着关于莱利先生所有值得知道的“内幕情报”。但莱利当时正春风得意，他叫你滚蛋，并让你带着你那廉价的敲诈伎俩一起滚。这对莱利来说就算解决了问题。从那时起，每周本杰·鲍威尔那份黄色小报《密勒氏评论报》或《字林西报》上都会提及莱利及其赌博事业。本杰和你都没能从莱利那里捞到一分钱，于是你们俩便以一种恶劣的方式对他穷追猛打——换言之，采用了典型的美国西部荒野风格。

好吧，莱利算是栽了，但你和贝杰并未因此经验而变得更富有。是的，阿尔，这又是一次倒霉的打击，试想一下，如果你得到了你以为即将到手的那笔钱，你会怎么花呢？祝你下次好运！

当然，电台“评论员”的工作还不错，能给你带来额外收入，且不考虑你必须自费雇佣的两名魁梧保镖，但战争很快就会由某一方获胜，而那个获胜者绝对不在支持你电台叫嚣的那帮人之中。也许你最好接受我们的建议，退出电台这一行，把你的肺留作其他用途——例如，为“飞力”及其他类似杀虫剂大喊广告。你知道，“飞力”等产品在消灭“害虫”方面非常有效。就个人而言，我们喜欢“飞力”，而且我们不会忘记用它来对付“害虫”，尤其是那种——嗓音粗嘎、体态邋遢的“害虫”。

再见！

朱尼厄斯·西尼库斯

LETTERS OF JUNIUS SINICUS 
; A NOTE TO THE READER 

Normally Junius Sinicus attempts to preserve in his communtica- 
tions a standard of lanquage and style not inconsistent with the name 
he has adopted. Even in his most abustve moments he has kept his 
abuse dignified, and has not descended to a mere vulgar and tgnor- 
ant calling of names. If, in the following letter, he departs from 
that rule, and adopts the language of the gutter, it is because he wishes 
his remarks to be’ understood by the individual to whom they are 
addressed, and any other locas would, it is feared, be far above his 
head. 


TO CARROLL D. ALCOTT, ESQ., 
Radio Commentator and Blackmailer, 
c/o “The China Press" . 
Shanghat. 
HoOwpy AL!—This, I believe, is how your fellow Americans usually 
address you, 30 lest you fail to recognize any more polite form 
of address I am adopting the same contemptuous tamiliarity. 

You will no doubt wonder what prompted. this letter. The fact 
is that the other day I came across in the dictionary, the word—PEST, 
meaning “Troublesume or destructive person, animal, or thing.’s and 
somehow I immediately thought of you. Before my mind’s eye ap- 
peared the face (or should I, to make sure you realiy understand, say 

“mug’’) of a slackly obese individual, who by some strange freak of 
Providence has been permitted to plague the community which he 
has infested. This may not speak very well for the community in 
question, but seeing that this very community contains a large pro- 
portion of parasitic, anaemic individuals who thrive on the offal 
which pests exude, it need not be a matter for great surprise, though 
it is certainly one for considerable ‘regret. 

In hygienic and well-ordered communities, pests are not. in the 
least welcome and I: for one am whole-heartedly for their extermin- 
ation here. You know, Al; you may be a little tin-god (or brass-horn) 
to some of your listeners-in, but not to all of them. Decent people 
like good clean things, not pests, and they cannot forget all the 

things of which you are a foul composition, which definitely place - 
you in the latter category. 


2 JUNIUS SINICUS 


When you first came here from some low dive in gangster-ridden 
Chicago, you were much slimmer, it is true, but you already had all 
the ear-marks of a pest, and a fairly poisoncus one at that. It 
did not take you very long to settle down to a racket. A gullible 
editor, American, of course, gave you a “lift”, and you were assigned 
to cover the courts. That was a Heaven-sent gift, as nothing could 
have suited your racket better. At that time, some fifteen years ago, 
there were still a few modest souls in this city who shrank from the 
glare of publicity, especially if this publicity arose from a divorce 
suit. These meek souls presented fine, red meat for you, the Rave- 
nous Pest. Your sharp ears listened avidly to all the evidence pro- 
duced in court, and all that was not told in court you obtained from 
unscrupulous lawyers (especially from a certain bearded specimen 
of the species). All the sordid details (including a great deal of 
imaginative matter divulged by embittered husbands, wives or third 
parties to the inevitable triangle) were carefully collected, after 
which you prepared for the kill. Silence and suppression of pub- 
licity were often very welcome to divorcing parties, and you did 
not have much difficulty 1. making them pay for suppression of the 
news in your bag. In fact, you usually got all the necessary dope 
beforehand from. the lawyers, and got your “fees” even before the 
court hearing. It was certainly a lovely racket, and an illustrious 
example of American journalism as practised by an illustrious mem- 
‘ber of the American Fourth Estate. 

Unfortunately for you, your racket di) not last very long. You 
got up against an irate husband once, a strong man who did not in 
the least care whether you published news of his divorce or not, and 
moreover, strongly objected to your blackmailing methods. Besides 
giving you a good hammering, he also reported your actions to the 
police. It was a matter of touch-and-go for you, and prison-bars 
leomed uncemfortably close, but some smart lying on your part, 
coupled with ‘“‘moral” support from the bearded lawyer referred to 
above, saved you from being a public liability. Some pests really 
bear charmed lives! ' ; 

Your narrow escape put the brakes on your unholy ambitions, 
and you tried te settle down to straight journalism. But it was 
tough going, Al, wasn’t it? No nice, fat pickings, and therefore no 


good whoopee times. Yes, it sure was tough! Banging away ‘ata. 


typewriter all day long (for a paltry 150 dollars a month), and 
parading the streets for n:-ws, was not at all to the liking of a Peat. 

Opportunity, however, came knocking round your door again 
pretty soon after that. Of course, Al, you remember your old pal

TO CARROLL D. ALCOTT 3 


Beaumont alias Israelovitch, (there always seems to be a little Jew 
about), and his high-powered manipulations in this city. Among 
Beaumont’s numerous ventures, which included motor-cycle dirt track 
speeding and cycle racing, (which flopped when he failed to obtain 
the license for pari-mutuels and other gambling devices from which 
he planned to make money), was a yellow sheet called the “Shanghai 
Spectator."” Your pal Beaumont had to beat it rather hastily one 
fine day, and left all his ventures in the gutter, so to speak, including 
his yellow sheet. It wasn’t a very difficult job for you to pick up 
the said yellow sheet, because, as we understand it, pests usually 
crawl in gutters. 

Thus, finally, your heart’s desire was satisfied, and we find a 
real, live pest seated in an editorial chair in a rather lousy, but still
